slides.kicker: Branding and AI · Chapter 20 · Appendix S1
slides.title: Product Requirements and Scope
slides.subtitle: The $100,000 no, and why the things you refuse to build define the product more than the things you build.

slides.title: Coherent the way a committee memo is coherent
slides.lead: Here is a thing that happens constantly in software teams. You start building without deciding in advance what you are building.
bullets: The engineer annoyed by the lack of multi-user accounts says yes and builds it. The PM who uses Notion says Notion. The person who gave the last demo adds custom feeds because the prospect asked.
By the time v1 ships — *if* it ships — the product is a collection of in-the-moment decisions made under different assumptions by people solving different problems.
A PRD is not a form you fill out before you are allowed to write code. **It is the mechanism by which you force yourself to make decisions before writing code.**
The decisions are hard. The PRD is what makes you make them.

slides.title: The PRD specifies the *what*, not the *how*
slides.lead: The product team decides what the product needs to do. The engineering team decides how to implement it. The boundary leaks in one direction, always.
slides.why: chapter draws the what/how line and names exactly the decisions that smuggle across it — '"via SendGrid at 7 a.m. Eastern using a Handlebars template" — this is how in what's clothing… The PRD should not specify the model, the temperature, or the prompt structure'

slides.title: One page. Four sections. Each answers one question.
slides.lead: Nothing advances until the section above it survives its own failure mode. Whether yours clears is not something this deck can tell you.
slides.why: chapter states 'The one-page PRD has four sections. Each answers one question' and then walks each in order with its characteristic failure mode — Problem, Gap, Tool, MVP Boundary

gates.label: Problem
gates.rule: a user, a task, a frequency, a cost

gates.label: Tool
gates.rule: an engineer can build it, a user can judge it

gates.label: MVP Boundary
gates.rule: the out list, with the $100,000 no at its head

slides.title: The market is either cheap-and-dumb or expensive-and-complex
slides.lead: "There are tools out there, but they're not quite right" is not a gap analysis. A gap analysis names actual products and explains exactly what each one gets wrong for *your* user.
slides.why: chapter names four competitors and a specific failure mode for each — Google Alerts free but no deduplication or scoring, Feedly Pro $8/month with no analysis layer, Brand24 from $99/month but enterprise-scoped, Crayon at $1,500/month minimum

slides.title: Five in. Eight out. The out list is the document.
slides.lead: Every PRD has an "in" list — that is the natural output of a feature brainstorm. The out list is what takes discipline, because every item on it is a thing someone on the team wanted.
slides.why: chapter prints both columns in full and counts them — 'That out list has eight items. Each one is a thing a reasonable user would want and a reasonable engineer would want to build. Each one is a door that will not be opened in v1.'

data.note: Each one is a door that will not be opened in v1.

slides.title: "Minimum" does not mean "the least possible"
slides.lead: It means the smallest thing that produces validated learning. Ries defined it precisely in 2011, and three words in that definition are doing serious work.
bullets: **Version** — a real product, not a mock. A Figma prototype gets you feedback on colours and layout. It will not tell you whether a marketing manager actually reads the sheet on a Tuesday morning with their real data.

**Validated** — the learning came from what users *did*, not what they *said*. "Would you use a tool that…" gets a yes from nearly everyone. "Did you open the Google Sheet three times last week?" gets an honest answer from the usage data.
**Learning** — you must know which assumption you are testing *before* you build. If you do not know what you are testing, you cannot interpret the result.
A manager who stops opening the sheet after two weeks is telling you one of three things: the intelligence is not actionable, the format is wrong, or the cadence is wrong. You need to know which.

slides.title: Hypothesis, Build, Measure, Learn — and back
slides.lead: The PRD's problem statement is what lets you formulate the hypothesis. The loop only works if the hypothesis existed before the build.
slides.why: chapter prints the loop as four numbered steps that return to the start — 'If open rate drops after week one, the problem was not the filtering — it was the format or the cadence. Update the hypothesis and rebuild' — with the PRD marked as a living document

edges.label: the smallest tool that tests it
do they open it? do they pay?

slides.section: why the boundary is the point
slides.title: A fat v1 buys you six months of learning nothing
slides.lead: The MVP boundary is what keeps the loop tight.
bullets: A PRD that puts too much in v1 takes six months to ship. **You learn nothing for six months.**
The competitor who shipped a worse product four months ago has already run three learn cycles and is now on v4. You are still on v1.
The discipline is uncomfortable because it means shipping something clearly incomplete. You *know* it needs multi-user accounts. You *know* the dashboard should beat a Google Sheet.
Until you have validated that someone will pay for the core thing, none of the additions matter. **Ship the core thing. Validate. Then add the layer.**

slides.title: Linear does fewer things, by design
slides.lead: Launched in 2019, grew through word-of-mouth among engineers, and reached a reported $35 million ARR by 2023 with a famously lean team.
bullets: Linear's team has repeatedly declined enterprise customization requests — including multi-workflow configurations worth significant annual contracts — because those customizations conflicted with the product philosophy.
*Opinionated software.* Teams that want to use Linear *their* way find the product resistant. Teams that adopt Linear's model find it exceptional.
*Simple and fast.* Every rejected customization is also a rejected source of UI complexity, backend branching logic and on-call incidents. **The no to the customer is simultaneously a yes to speed.**
Engineers recommend it to other engineers not because it has more features — it has fewer — but because the constraints produce a coherent experience.

slides.title: Scope discipline compounds. So does its absence.
slides.lead: Each refusal preserves the coherence that made the product worth using. Over time the coherence becomes the identity, and the identity becomes the brand.
slides.why: chapter's own chart is two lines from a shared origin — 'scope discipline held' rising against 'feature requests accepted' falling, with the divergence labelled as the moment the gap becomes brand identity

tracks.label: Refused · discipline held
notes: fewer surfaces, so it ships more often
users arrive who value exactly that

tracks.label: Accepted · coherence spent for cash
notes: the original users quietly move on

slides.title: Not "I will not build things that are out of scope"
slides.lead: Every product has out-of-scope things by default. That is not a discipline. The $100,000 no is the feature you would decline even if declining cost you something real.
bullets: A real user will ask for it, with a real argument for why it belongs. They will have a budget. The implementation is not technically difficult.

For a sentiment pipeline aimed at small marketing teams, it might be **multi-user accounts** — because that changes the product from a personal intelligence tool into a team platform, and those are different products.
The day you build it, every subsequent decision — permissions, audit trails, team dashboards, admin interfaces — is a team-platform decision. **The product's point of view has changed.**
Write your $100,000 no *before* you write the rest of the PRD. Put it in the out-of-scope column, first. Then write the document around it.

slides.title: From a wish to a spec, one discard at a time
slides.lead: The worked example does not arrive at the problem statement. It fails its way there, twice, on the record.
slides.why: chapter's own figure calls this the PRD rewrite ladder — attempt 1 'a wish. It has no user, no frequency, no cost. Discard it'; attempt 2 'still too abstract… Discard it'; attempt 3 'Now we have something… It is testable.'

rungs.label: Attempt 1
rungs.note: "Marketing professionals need better competitive intelligence." No user, no frequency, no cost.

rungs.label: Attempt 2
rungs.note: "Small marketing teams lack good competitive intelligence tools." Not a person; an absence, not a pain.

rungs.label: Attempt 3
rungs.note: A named user, a Monday, two to three hours, a reason no existing tool fits their price point.

slides.title: A contract with future-you
slides.lead: A record of the decisions you made when you were thinking clearly, preserved for the moment when you are thinking under pressure.
slides.why: chapter registers the commitment ahead of the evidence — 'The pressure will come. The contract is what keeps you from agreeing to things you will regret' — and never says whether yours holds

marks.label: a real user asks for it

slides.title: Where I would be wrong, and what I still cannot teach
slides.lead: The argument here is theoretical and industrial. The experimental evidence in student contexts is thin.
bullets: **What would change my mind:** a controlled study comparing cohorts who wrote a PRD before building against cohorts who did not, measuring time-to-ship and retention at thirty days. If the no-PRD group ships faster *and* retains longer, this appendix should be removed. **I have not run the study.**
**Still puzzling:** the exact moment scope discipline tips from useful constraint into creative restriction.

Linear's discipline works because it is grounded in a coherent point of view. A student without one, practising the same discipline, ends up refusing features for no good reason — a sterile discipline rather than a productive one.
I teach the $100,000 no as a tool. What I have not figured out is how to teach the point of view that makes the no meaningful rather than merely rigid.

slides.title: Write the refusal first.
slides.lead: One page. Four sections. A problem statement you had to discard twice to get right. A gap analysis with named competitors and named failures. An out list at least as long as the in list, each item carrying the archetype reason it was refused — and your $100,000 no at its head. Then hold it when the argument and the budget arrive. Every grey slot on this deck is a verdict only your own PRD can settle.
